explanation: Placing separate bars side-by-side within each category allows direct comparison of sub-groups like age categories across clinics. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h3)

question: When should you choose a bar chart instead of a line graph?

options.A: When displaying continuous patient temperature changes hourly
options.B: When comparing distinct categories rather than time trends
options.C: When tracking blood pressure fluctuations over a 24-hour period
options.D: When measuring exact body weight changes across weeks

explanation: Bar charts display separate groups, whereas line graphs are specifically designed to track continuous progression over time. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which graph type should you use to display continuous numerical data like age distribution?

options.A: Pictogram
options.B: Bar chart
options.C: Histogram
options.D: Pie chart

explanation: Histograms feature touching bars to represent continuous numerical data intervals, unlike the separated bars of a bar chart. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h4)

question: What number should the numerical scale on the Y-axis of a standard bar chart always start at?

options.A: One
options.B: Zero
options.C: The median value
options.D: The lowest data value

explanation: Starting the Y-axis at zero prevents visual distortion of the bar heights and maintains accurate proportional representation. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h5)

question: What is the first step when preparing to draw a bar chart from raw research data?

options.A: Organize raw numbers into a frequency table
options.B: Write the detailed conclusion paragraph
options.C: Draw the horizontal baseline axis first
options.D: Choose bright colors for every single bar

explanation: Before drawing any graphics, the raw data must be tallied and structured into clear categories and counts. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h5)

question: What happens when you read a bar chart where the Y-axis does not start at zero?

options.A: The total number of patients surveyed becomes impossible to count
options.B: The chart automatically converts into a continuous histogram
options.C: The category names on the horizontal axis disappear entirely
options.D: Small differences between groups can look massively exaggerated

explanation: Truncating the baseline distorts proportions, making minor numerical variations appear dramatically larger than they actually are. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h6)

question: What part of a bar chart should you look at first to understand its context?

options.A: The title and axis labels
options.B: The color of the shortest bar
options.C: The software brand used to draw it
options.D: The blank space around the graph

explanation: Titles and labels provide essential background information regarding what data, population, and units are being measured. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why should a nurse researcher avoid using complex 3D visual effects on a simple bar chart?

options.A: Three-dimensional charts are strictly illegal in academic journal publications
options.B: Three-dimensional effects can distort data and make values hard to read
options.C: Three-dimensional graphics require specialized mathematical formulas to print
options.D: Three-dimensional bars automatically change the category names

explanation: Unnecessary 3D shading skews perspective, making it difficult to match bar heights accurately with the vertical axis scale. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h7)

question: Which of the following is poor practice when designing a bar chart?

options.A: Keeping category labels on the horizontal axis clear
options.B: Using inconsistent bar widths for different categories
options.C: Using simple, clean colors for the rectangular bars
options.D: Starting the vertical frequency axis at zero

explanation: Bar widths must remain uniform so that viewers judge values by height rather than accidentally comparing total area. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h7)

question: What shape does a pie chart traditionally use to display data?

options.A: A round circle
options.B: A jagged triangle
options.C: A long rectangle
options.D: A square box

explanation: A pie chart is represented as a circular graph divided into proportional slices. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h1)

question: Why do nurses use visual data presentation tools like pie charts during ward meetings?

options.A: To calculate daily drug dosages for severe malaria cases
options.B: To make raw hospital figures easier to understand quickly
options.C: To hide missing patient statistics from the medical director
options.D: To replace every written nursing care plan in the folder

explanation: Visual charts translate complex numbers into simple proportions for fast clinical interpretation. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h1)

question: What does the entire circle of a pie chart represent in a dataset?

options.A: Ten percent of the measured variables
options.B: The average age of all admitted staff
options.C: Only the male patients in the ward
options.D: One hundred percent of the total data

explanation: The full pie equals the complete total of all categories combined, which equals one hundred percent. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h2)

question: A clinic records 50 malaria cases out of a total 200 patient visits. What percentage of the total visits is this?

options.A: Ten percent
options.B: Fifty percent
options.C: Seventy-five percent
options.D: Twenty-five percent

explanation: Dividing 50 by 200 gives 0.25, which converts to twenty-five percent. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h2)

question: Which nursing dataset is most suitable for display in a pie chart?

options.A: Weight changes of infants measured every month for a year
options.B: Hourly temperature readings of a typhoid patient for two days
options.C: Daily patient admission numbers recorded over a twelve-month period
options.D: Blood groups of pregnant women attending antenatal care

explanation: Pie charts suit categorical data with a small number of groups rather than continuous time-series data. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h3)

question: What is the recommended maximum number of categories to keep a pie chart readable?

options.A: Exactly two categories
options.B: Fifty separate groups
options.C: Six or fewer categories
options.D: Up to twenty categories

explanation: Too many slices crowd the chart and make visual comparison very difficult. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h3)

question: How many total degrees make up the full area of a circle in a pie chart?

options.A: Ninety degrees
options.B: One hundred eighty degrees
options.C: One thousand degrees
options.D: Three hundred sixty degrees

explanation: A complete circle always measures 360 degrees around its center point. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h4)

question: A category represents twenty-five percent of a dataset. How many degrees should its slice measure on a pie chart?

options.A: Three hundred sixty degrees
options.B: Forty-five degrees
options.C: Ninety degrees
options.D: One hundred eighty degrees

explanation: Multiplying twenty-five percent or 0.25 by 360 degrees gives 90 degrees. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h4)

question: What drawing instrument is used to measure accurate slice angles on a paper pie chart?

options.A: A stethoscope
options.B: A protractor
options.C: A thermometer
options.D: A surgical scalpel

explanation: A protractor is the standard geometric tool used for measuring and drawing angles in degrees. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h5)

question: What does the largest slice on a healthcare pie chart typically indicate?

options.A: The smallest group of patients sampled in the hospital
options.B: Data that should be excluded from the final research report
options.C: The most frequent condition or category in the study
options.D: An error made during the mathematical degree calculation

explanation: Larger angles correspond to higher frequencies, highlighting the dominant category in the dataset. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h5)

question: What is a major limitation of using pie charts in research reports?

options.A: They can only display data that adds up to exactly ten items
options.B: The human eye struggles to compare similar-sized slice angles accurately
options.C: They require measuring temperatures rather than counting patient numbers
options.D: They are completely impossible to generate using computer software

explanation: Visual estimation of angles is less precise than comparing bar lengths on a standard bar chart. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h6)

question: Why might a nurse researcher choose a bar chart over a pie chart?

options.A: To hide total patient numbers from the hospital ethics committee
options.B: To ensure the final research paper has no visual illustrations
options.C: To represent data that represents a single 360-degree circle
options.D: To compare many different categories or values with similar sizes easily

explanation: Bar charts make comparing heights or lengths much easier than comparing pie slices. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h6)

question: Why should nurses avoid using 3D effects on pie charts in research presentations?

options.A: They automatically change the total circle measurement from 360 to 180 degrees
options.B: They prevent the calculation of correct percentage values
options.C: They distort visual proportions and make front slices look deceptively large
options.D: They increase the physical weight of the printed research document

explanation: Three-dimensional perspective skew distorts data visualization, misleading the reader about true proportions. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h7)

question: What should all the individual percentage slices in a correct pie chart add up to?

options.A: Three hundred sixty percent
options.B: One hundred percent
options.C: One thousand percent
options.D: Fifty percent

explanation: The sum of all parts in a complete pie chart must equal the whole, which is one hundred percent. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T8#GNS217_U4_T8_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a histogram in research data analysis?

options.A: To track individual patient treatment progress over time
options.B: To visualize the distribution of numerical data
options.C: To compare two entirely different categorical groups
options.D: To calculate the exact mean of a small sample

explanation: Histograms group continuous numerical data into intervals to display frequency distributions clearly. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h1)

question: A researcher wants to show the spread of patient ages in a ward. Why choose a histogram?

options.A: It outlines exact individual patient names and ages clearly
options.B: it completely eliminates the need for calculating percentages
options.C: It proves cause and effect between age and recovery rate
options.D: It displays how continuous data frequencies cluster across ranges

explanation: Grouping continuous data into intervals allows researchers to see patterns and clusters in the population. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h1)

question: Why do the bars on a histogram touch each other?

options.A: Categorical variables require connected visual rectangles
options.B: There are not enough data points to create spacing
options.C: The data on the horizontal axis is continuous
options.D: The software used to draw them has formatting errors

explanation: Touching bars indicate that the measurement scale is continuous with no gaps between intervals. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h2)

question: What does the height of a specific bar represent on a histogram?

options.A: The maximum possible limit of the measured variable
options.B: The number of observations falling within that bin's range
options.C: The average value of all numbers inside that interval
options.D: The total sum of all measurements combined together

explanation: The vertical axis measures frequency, so taller bars mean more data points landed in that specific range. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h2)

question: Which of the following features is TRUE for a standard bar chart?

options.A: The horizontal axis represents numerical intervals
options.B: It is used exclusively for continuous numerical scales
options.C: Spaces exist clearly between the individual bars
options.D: The bars must always touch each other without gaps

explanation: Bar charts display categorical data, using spaces between bars to show separate groups. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h3)

question: A nurse wants to graph blood pressure readings versus types of ward admissions. Which chart applies to blood pressure?

options.A: A histogram, because blood pressure uses continuous numerical values
options.B: A bar chart, because blood pressure readings are categories
options.C: A pie chart, because readings can be broken into percentages
options.D: Any chart works equally well for both data types

explanation: Continuous measurements like blood pressure require histograms to show interval frequencies properly. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h3)

question: What is the very first step when creating a frequency histogram?

options.A: Draw the vertical frequency axis on graph paper
options.B: Determine the number of categories needed for bars
options.C: Calculate the exact average of all available values
options.D: Collect the numerical data from your study or audit

explanation: You must first gather your measurements before you can calculate ranges or draw bins. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h4)

question: Why must the bins or intervals on a histogram be equal in width?

options.A: To make the final graph look colorful and appealing
options.B: To eliminate the need for a vertical frequency axis
options.C: To ensure that every single data point equals zero
options.D: To prevent misrepresentation of data frequencies across the scale

explanation: Unequal bin widths distort the visual height of bars, making data look falsely compressed or expanded. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h4)

question: A patient length-of-stay histogram shows a long tail trailing to the right. What does this mean?

options.A: The data was collected incorrectly and lacks any clinical value
options.B: Most patients stay a short time, with a few staying very long
options.C: Most patients remain admitted for unusually long periods
options.D: Patients stay for equal durations across all measured intervals

explanation: A right skew indicates a cluster of low values with a small number of high-value outliers pulling the tail right. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h5)

question: What does a symmetrical, bell-shaped histogram indicate about a dataset?

options.A: All recorded values are completely identical to each other
options.B: Most data points cluster in the middle with balanced tails
options.C: The data contains severe errors and extreme outliers
options.D: The measurements were taken using categorical variables

explanation: Symmetry means observations are evenly distributed around a central peak. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h5)

question: A nurse manager wants to evaluate emergency room waiting times against policy standards. Which tool is best suited?

options.A: A pie chart to show the percentage of nurses on duty
options.B: A histogram to display the frequency distribution of wait times
options.C: A scatter plot to compare patient age with blood type
options.D: A line graph to show individual patient medical history

explanation: Wait times are continuous numerical data, making histograms ideal for checking performance against standards. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h6)

question: How do histograms assist nurse leaders in quality improvement projects?

options.A: They guarantee that clinical errors will never happen again
options.B: They reveal performance patterns and process variations quickly
options.C: They punish staff members who make medication administration errors
options.D: They replace the need for writing formal incident reports

explanation: Visualizing data spread helps leaders identify systemic issues like excessive waiting times or dosing errors. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T9#GNS217_U4_T9_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of a research design in nursing studies?

options.A: To determine the final cost of publishing the research paper
options.B: To serve as a structural blueprint for conducting the study
options.C: To select the statistical software used for data analysis
options.D: To recruit patients from hospital wards for clinical trials

explanation: A research design acts as the foundational plan that guides the entire execution of a study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why must a nurse researcher carefully align the research design with the clinical question?

options.A: To guarantee the study receives immediate international funding
options.B: To eliminate the need for an institutional ethics review committee
options.C: To reduce the total number of participants required for testing
options.D: To ensure the collected data accurately answers the specific clinical inquiry

explanation: The chosen design dictates how data is gathered, meaning it must match the specific goals of the research question. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h1)

question: What is the primary focus of quantitative research designs in healthcare?

options.A: Detailed personal stories of chronic illness
options.B: Historical archives of nursing leadership
options.C: Subjective emotional experiences of grief
options.D: Numerical data and objective measurement

explanation: Quantitative research relies heavily on numbers, statistics, and measurable variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h2)

question: A study measures the relationship between hours of sleep and stress levels without manipulating any variables. What design is this?

options.A: Qualitative phenomenological
options.B: Correlational quantitative
options.C: True experimental
options.D: Randomized controlled trial

explanation: Correlational designs examine the association between variables without introducing an active intervention. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which research design focuses primarily on understanding the lived experiences of individuals?

options.A: Correlational
options.B: Phenomenology
options.C: Cross-sectional
options.D: Experimental

explanation: Phenomenological studies explore the subjective, lived realities of people experiencing specific life events. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h3)

question: A nurse wants to explore how traditional birth attendants perceive modern obstetric care in a rural Nigerian community. Which design fits best?

options.A: Descriptive statistics
options.B: Ethnography
options.C: Randomized trial
options.D: Cohort analysis

explanation: Ethnography involves studying cultural groups and their shared patterns and perspectives within their natural environment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h3)

question: What is the key feature that distinguishes an experimental design from a non-experimental design?

options.A: The total absence of any statistical data analysis
options.B: Active manipulation of an independent variable by the researcher
options.C: Conducting the study outside of a hospital environment
options.D: Relying exclusively on historical patient records

explanation: Experimental designs require the researcher to introduce an intervention or treatment to measure its effect. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why might a nurse choose a non-experimental design instead of an experimental one?

options.A: Patients refuse to participate in experimental protocols
options.B: Non-experimental studies always provide stronger proof of causality
options.C: Experimental designs cannot be published in nursing journals
options.D: Manipulating the variable of interest is unethical or impossible

explanation: Researchers cannot experimentally manipulate harmful exposures or certain patient behaviors, requiring observational designs instead. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which epidemiological study design compares patients with a specific disease to healthy controls by looking backward in time?

options.A: Case-control study
options.B: Randomized trial
options.C: Cohort study
options.D: Cross-sectional survey

explanation: Case-control studies start with the outcome and look backward to identify past exposures. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h5)

question: A researcher follows a group of nurses over ten years to see if shift work leads to hypertension. What design is this?

options.A: Phenomenological study
options.B: Case-control study
options.C: Cohort study
options.D: Qualitative interview

explanation: Cohort studies follow exposure-defined groups forward in time to observe the development of health outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h5)

question: What does a mixed methods research design combine?

options.A: Historical and future projections
options.B: Inpatient and outpatient records
options.C: Animal and human laboratory trials
options.D: Quantitative and qualitative data

explanation: Mixed methods research integrates numerical data with subjective, narrative data in a single study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h6)

question: Why is a mixed methods design particularly useful in complex clinical nursing studies?

options.A: It completely eliminates the possibility of human error
options.B: It explains statistical findings with rich experiential context
options.C: It reduces the financial cost of research to zero
options.D: It removes the need for institutional ethical approval

explanation: Combining both paradigms allows researchers to measure outcomes numerically while exploring the human meaning behind those numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h6)

question: What type of validity refers to whether study findings can be generalized to other patient populations?

options.A: External validity
options.B: Sampling reliability
options.C: Measurement bias
options.D: Internal validity

explanation: External validity deals with the applicability of research results to broader real-world settings and populations. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why is identifying potential bias in a research design critical for clinical practice?

options.A: Bias can systematically skew results and lead to ineffective patient care
options.B: Bias proves that the researchers used qualitative interviewing methods
options.C: Bias guarantees that the study will receive international funding
options.D: Bias automatically increases the sample size of the participant pool

explanation: Uncontrolled bias distorts study conclusions, making interventions appear more or less effective than they actually are. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T1#GNS224_U1_T1_h7)

question: What defines a cross-sectional research design regarding time?

options.A: Data is gathered retrospectively from old hospital files
options.B: Data is collected at one specific point in time
options.C: Data is collected over a period of ten years
options.D: Data is collected prospectively after a clinical intervention

explanation: Cross-sectional studies examine a population at a single, defined moment, acting like a snapshot. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why is a cross-sectional study likened to a photographic snapshot?

options.A: It requires expensive high-resolution camera equipment
options.B: It produces visual graphs instead of statistical tables
options.C: It captures a population status at one moment
options.D: It permanently freezes cellular tissue for laboratory analysis

explanation: The snapshot analogy highlights that the design captures variables at one single point without showing past or future changes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which feature is always absent in a cross-sectional study?

options.A: Calculation of disease prevalence rates
options.B: Researcher manipulation of the study variable
options.C: Involvement of human human participants
options.D: Use of structured questionnaires or surveys

explanation: Cross-sectional studies are purely observational, meaning researchers do not administer treatments or manipulate conditions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h2)

question: When is a cross-sectional study classified as analytical rather than purely descriptive?

options.A: When it excludes all quantitative data in favor of audio interviews
options.B: When the researcher introduces a new nursing care protocol
options.C: When it follows the patient cohort for at least five years
options.D: When it examines statistical associations between exposures and outcomes

explanation: Analytical cross-sectional studies go beyond simple counts to test relationships between risk factors and health conditions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the very first step when planning a cross-sectional study?

options.A: Entering numerical data into computer software
options.B: Defining the specific research question
options.C: Publishing the final article in a nursing journal
options.D: Applying for ethical clearance from the hospital board

explanation: Every research project must begin with a clear research question that guides the population selection and data gathering methods. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h3)

question: A nurse researcher wants to study hypertension prevalence in a rural market. What should be done immediately after defining the population?

options.A: Calculate the required sample size
options.B: Destroy all collected survey papers
options.C: Begin treating patients with antihypertensive drugs
options.D: Write the concluding discussion section

explanation: Determining the sample size follows population definition to ensure enough participants are recruited for valid statistical power. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h3)

question: What data collection method is often best for populations with low literacy levels?

options.A: Automated computer terminal logs
options.B: Complex self-administered postal questionnaires
options.C: Online Google survey links
options.D: Structured face-to-face interviews

explanation: Interviews allow researchers to read questions aloud and clarify meanings for participants who might struggle with written forms. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h4)

question: Why must data collection instruments be both valid and reliable in cross-sectional research?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any statistical analysis later
options.B: To guarantee the research receives international grant funding
options.C: To reduce the total number of survey questions by half
options.D: To ensure they accurately measure what is intended consistently

explanation: Validity and reliability guarantee that the single snapshot of data collected actually reflects true clinical realities. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which statistical measure is commonly used to report disease frequency in cross-sectional studies?

options.A: Survival time
options.B: Incidence rate
options.C: Mortality hazard
options.D: Prevalence

explanation: Cross-sectional studies measure existing cases at one point, which gives the prevalence of the condition rather than its new incidence. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why is it incorrect to claim causation from a statistically significant cross-sectional association?

options.A: Statistical software packages cannot calculate causal pathways
options.B: Exposure and outcome are measured at the exact same time
options.C: Ethics committees forbid the use of regression models
options.D: Sample sizes in cross-sectional studies are always too small

explanation: Simultaneous measurement makes it impossible to know whether the exposure preceded the outcome or vice versa. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is a major advantage of cross-sectional research designs?

options.A: They require no ethical clearance from institutional boards
options.B: They track patient health outcomes over many decades
options.C: They are relatively quick and cost-effective to conduct
options.D: They prove definitive cause and effect relationships

explanation: Because data is gathered all at once without follow-up periods, these studies save both time and financial resources. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of cross-sectional studies?

options.A: High susceptibility to loss to follow-up over time
options.B: Vulnerability to recall bias from survey participants
options.C: Difficulty investigating rare health conditions
options.D: Inability to establish clear temporal sequence or causation

explanation: Loss to follow-up is a problem in longitudinal or cohort studies, not cross-sectional studies where participants are contacted only once. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h6)

question: A Nigerian nurse manager needs a quick assessment of ward supply shortages to present to the hospital board next week. Which study design is most appropriate?

options.A: Randomized controlled trial
options.B: Ten-year cohort study
options.C: Retrospective case-control study
options.D: Cross-sectional survey

explanation: A cross-sectional survey delivers rapid data necessary for immediate administrative planning and resource allocation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h7)

question: How do cross-sectional studies directly support community health nursing in Nigeria?

options.A: By identifying local disease burdens to target public health interventions
options.B: By proving genetic causes of inherited tropical diseases
options.C: By following individual patients from birth until old age
options.D: By testing new surgical techniques in major teaching hospitals

explanation: Community health nurses use prevalence data from cross-sectional surveys to plan effective outreach and educational programs. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T10#GNS224_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary feature of a longitudinal research design?

options.A: Intervening directly in a patient's medical treatment
options.B: Collecting data from the same participants repeatedly over time
options.C: Comparing two different groups at a single point in time
options.D: Reviewing past medical records without patient contact

explanation: Longitudinal research focuses on tracking identical subjects across multiple time points to observe changes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers choose longitudinal designs over cross-sectional studies?

options.A: To eliminate all possibilities of participant drop-out during the study
options.B: To measure changes and developments within the same individuals over time
options.C: To avoid the need for ethical approval from institutional review boards
options.D: To finish the research project much faster with lower financial costs

explanation: Observing the same group repeatedly allows researchers to track individual trajectories and developmental changes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h1)

question: Which longitudinal study type follows the exact same sample of individuals over time?

options.A: Cross-sectional study
options.B: Panel study
options.C: Case-control study
options.D: Trend study

explanation: Panel studies track the identical set of participants across multiple observation periods. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h2)

question: How does a trend study differ from a panel study?

options.A: Trend studies focus exclusively on historical medical records
options.B: Trend studies require no interaction with human participants
options.C: Trend studies sample different people from the same population over time
options.D: Trend studies only collect data at a single point in time

explanation: Trend designs look at shifts in a general population by drawing new samples at each interval. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is a major advantage of longitudinal research in healthcare?

options.A: Completing data collection within a few hours or days
options.B: Establishing the chronological sequence of events for causality
options.C: Guaranteeing zero participant drop-out throughout the study
options.D: Eliminating the need to recruit human participants

explanation: Tracking subjects over time lets researchers see what happens before and after an event, clarifying cause and effect. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is capturing intra-individual change important for nursing care?

options.A: It prevents patients from developing chronic illnesses
options.B: It shows how a health condition progresses or improves within a specific person
options.C: It allows nurses to compare entirely different communities at once
options.D: It removes the need for statistical data analysis software

explanation: Intra-individual tracking highlights personal trajectories of healing or disease worsening over time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h3)

question: What term describes the loss of study participants over time in longitudinal research?

options.A: Blinding
options.B: Attrition
options.C: Stratification
options.D: Randomization

explanation: Attrition refers to participants dropping out or being lost to follow-up during a long-term study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why is participant attrition a serious threat to longitudinal study validity?

options.A: It automatically increases the financial budget of the research project
options.B: Those who drop out may differ systematically from those who stay
options.C: It prevents the researcher from ever publishing the study results
options.D: It proves that the nursing intervention was completely unsuccessful

explanation: If a specific type of patient leaves the study, the remaining sample no longer represents the original population accurately. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h4)

question: Which strategy helps improve participant retention in long-term studies?

options.A: Collecting detailed alternate contact information during recruitment
options.B: Changing the research topic entirely at each observation point
options.C: Isolating participants so they cannot communicate with researchers
options.D: Stopping all communication between scheduled data collection waves

explanation: Having multiple ways to reach participants prevents them from being lost to follow-up when they move or change phone numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h5)

question: How do financial incentives and transportation reimbursements affect longitudinal studies?

options.A: They replace the need for ethical board review approval
options.B: They invalidate the study findings by biasing patient responses
options.C: They reduce attrition by removing practical barriers to participation
options.D: They guarantee that every participant will remain healthy

explanation: Compensating participants for time and travel expenses encourages them to return for subsequent data collection waves. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is informed consent considered in the context of longitudinal studies?

options.A: A verbal agreement that never requires documentation
options.B: An unnecessary administrative task once funding is approved
options.C: An ongoing, continuous process throughout the study duration
options.D: A single document signed only at the final data collection wave

explanation: Participants must be kept informed and re-consented as studies progress over months or years. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h6)

question: What ethical obligation does a nurse researcher have if a survey reveals a worsening condition?

options.A: Remove the participant from the research database immediately without help
options.B: Ensure the participant receives appropriate medical referral and care
options.C: Ignore the finding to maintain the objective data of the study
options.D: Publish the patient's personal medical details in a public journal

explanation: Patient welfare and duty of care always supersede research data collection protocols when urgent health needs arise. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T11#GNS224_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the main characteristic of a correlational research design?

options.A: Observing relationships without manipulation
options.B: Assigning patients to random groups
options.C: Manipulating an independent variable
options.D: Testing a new surgical procedure

explanation: Correlational studies observe variables naturally without the researcher interfering or changing them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why would a nurse researcher choose a correlational design instead of an experimental one?

options.A: To save money on hospital equipment
options.B: To test the effectiveness of a new drug
options.C: To prove that one variable causes another
options.D: When manipulating variables is unethical or impossible

explanation: Variables like smoking habits or stress levels cannot always be ethically manipulated, making observation necessary. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h1)

question: What happens in a negative correlation between two variables?

options.A: One variable increases while the other decreases
options.B: There is no relationship between them
options.C: Both variables increase together
options.D: Both variables decrease together

explanation: In a negative correlation, the two variables move in opposite directions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h2)

question: A study finds that as hourly fluid intake goes up, patient edema scores go down. What type of correlation is this?

options.A: Positive correlation
options.B: Spurious correlation
options.C: Negative correlation
options.D: Zero correlation

explanation: Because one variable increases while the other decreases, the relationship is negative. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h2)

question: What does a correlation coefficient of 0.00 indicate?

options.A: An error in data collection
options.B: A strong negative relationship
options.C: No linear relationship between variables
options.D: A perfect positive relationship

explanation: A coefficient of zero means there is no linear pattern connecting the two variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which correlation coefficient shows the strongest relationship between two clinical variables?
explanation: The absolute value furthest from zero represents the strongest relationship, ignoring the positive or negative sign. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h3)

question: What is a major advantage of correlational research in nursing?

options.A: It proves which nursing intervention works best
options.B: It requires very small sample sizes
options.C: It allows the study of variables in natural settings
options.D: It eliminates all potential confounding variables

explanation: Correlational studies observe real-world phenomena without artificial laboratory constraints. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why can a correlational study NOT establish cause and effect?

options.A: Statistical software cannot calculate causation
options.B: Sample sizes are always too small
options.C: There is no researcher manipulation or control of variables
options.D: Data is usually collected over too many years

explanation: Without actively manipulating the independent variable and controlling extraneous factors, causation cannot be proven. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h4)

question: What does finding a strong correlation between two variables actually prove?

options.A: The two variables are associated
options.B: An intervention is effective
options.C: The study results are biased
options.D: One variable causes the other

explanation: Correlation only shows that variables are related, not that one causes the other. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why is the phrase 'correlation does not equal causation' vital for clinical practice?

options.A: It ensures nurses do not change care based on mere associations
options.B: It means all clinical studies are invalid
options.C: It proves that statistical software is unreliable
options.D: It prevents nurses from reading research articles

explanation: Assuming an association is a cause can lead to ineffective or harmful changes in patient care protocols. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T12#GNS224_U1_T12_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of explanatory research design in healthcare?

options.A: To uncover cause and effect relationships
options.B: To count the prevalence of a disease
options.C: To observe daily nursing routines quietly
options.D: To test a brand new hospital machine

explanation: Explanatory research specifically focuses on discovering why phenomena occur by identifying underlying causes and effects. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h1)

question: How does explanatory research differ from a purely observational study?

options.A: It looks for underlying reasons behind health trends
options.B: It focuses solely on historical nursing events
options.C: It only happens inside a laboratory setting
options.D: It avoids collecting numerical data from patients

explanation: Observational studies only record what is present, whereas explanatory research investigates the underlying drivers of those observations. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h1)

question: The main objective of explanatory nursing research is establishing what?

options.A: The market price of common surgical equipment
options.B: Patient satisfaction scores across private hospitals
options.C: Clear causal links between interventions and outcomes
options.D: The exact number of nurses working night shifts

explanation: Establishing how specific nursing actions directly influence patient recovery is the core purpose of this design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h2)

question: Why is explanatory research valuable for evidence-based nursing practice?

options.A: It lowers the overall cost of running a nursing school
options.B: It replaces the need for clinical judgment entirely
options.C: It proves which clinical methods actually improve patient healing
options.D: It stops patients from asking questions about their care

explanation: Evidence-based practice relies on solid proof that a specific nursing intervention causes a positive health outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h2)

question: A core assumption of explanatory research is that clinical events follow what pattern?

options.A: Strictly seasonal weather changes
options.B: Predictable patterns of cause and effect
options.C: Completely random and chaotic cycles
options.D: Unrelated historical coincidence

explanation: The design assumes that health outcomes are direct results of preceding factors and can be systematically studied. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h3)

question: Why is structural control necessary in explanatory studies?

options.A: To rule out outside factors affecting the patient outcome
options.B: To make patients follow hospital rules more strictly
options.C: To ensure the research paper is written very quickly
options.D: To reduce the number of nurses needed on duty

explanation: Controlling the environment ensures that the observed changes are genuinely caused by the studied variable and nothing else. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h3)

question: When is an exploratory research design most appropriate to use?

options.A: When auditing financial records of a teaching hospital
options.B: When proving a strict cause and effect relationship
options.C: When calculating the exact dosage of a common drug
options.D: When very little is known about the health problem

explanation: Exploratory studies are designed for new or poorly understood topics where researchers are just starting to gather preliminary insights. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h4)

question: How does a descriptive study differ from an explanatory study?

options.A: Descriptive studies use experiments while explanatory studies only use surveys
options.B: Descriptive studies focus on the future while explanatory studies look at the past
options.C: Descriptive studies require patient consent while explanatory studies do not
options.D: Descriptive studies show what is happening while explanatory studies show why

explanation: Descriptive research outlines characteristics of a population, whereas explanatory research investigates the causal reasons behind those characteristics. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h4)

question: In an explanatory study, what does the independent variable represent?

options.A: The presumed cause of the change
options.B: The final outcome being measured
options.C: The demographic background of staff
options.D: The accidental error in data entry

explanation: The independent variable is manipulated or observed as the driving factor that brings about an effect on the dependent variable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h5)

question: A researcher studies how hand hygiene education impacts infection rates. What is the dependent variable?

options.A: The time of day the class is taught
options.B: The nursing license of the instructor
options.C: The hand hygiene education class
options.D: The patient infection rates

explanation: The infection rate is the outcome being measured to see if it responds to the education intervention. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h5)

question: What type of data is primarily collected in explanatory research designs?

options.A: Purely historical narratives
options.B: Unfiltered emotional opinions
options.C: Quantitative numerical data
options.D: Unstructured personal diaries

explanation: Explanatory studies rely on numbers and statistical measurements to accurately assess relationships between variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h6)

question: Why are standardized measurement tools essential during data collection?

options.A: They guarantee that every patient will be fully cured
options.B: They make patients finish answering questions much faster
options.C: They eliminate the need for ethical research approval
options.D: They ensure the collected data is reliable and valid

explanation: Using consistent tools ensures that measurements are accurate and free from unnecessary personal bias by the researcher. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h6)

question: Which statistical method is commonly used to examine causal relationships in explanatory research?

options.A: Patient census counting
options.B: Qualitative thematic sorting
options.C: Regression analysis
options.D: Handwritten tally marks

explanation: Regression analysis helps researchers understand how the typical value of the dependent variable changes when any one of the independent variables is varied. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of using inferential statistics in explanatory data analysis?

options.A: To make the research report look longer and more complex
options.B: To determine if findings happened by chance or are real
options.C: To increase the financial funding of the hospital ward
options.D: To hide missing data points from the ethics committee

explanation: Inferential statistics help test hypotheses and calculate probabilities to see if the observed results reflect true clinical relationships. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h7)

question: A major strength of explanatory research design is that it provides strong evidence for what?

options.A: Medical insurance pricing
options.B: Clinical decision-making
options.C: Nursing uniform selection
options.D: Hospital architectural design

explanation: The robust cause-and-effect evidence generated helps clinicians choose therapies that deliver proven patient outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common limitation of explanatory research designs?

options.A: They require careful management of confounding variables
options.B: They can feel artificial due to strict laboratory control
options.C: They perfectly reflect chaotic real-world hospital environments
options.D: They may pose ethical challenges when withholding standard care

explanation: High control often makes explanatory studies artificial rather than reflective of messy everyday clinical practice, which is a known limitation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary starting point for a retrospective research design?

options.A: A prospective patient interview process
options.B: A newly planned clinical intervention
options.C: An outcome that has already occurred
options.D: An active laboratory experiment on animals

explanation: Retrospective studies look backward in time from an established outcome to find preceding causes or factors. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h1)

question: How does a retrospective study differ fundamentally from a prospective study?

options.A: It looks at past events instead of following subjects forward.
options.B: It only uses qualitative interviews instead of quantitative data.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any ethical clearance approval.
options.D: It requires direct patient participation and live clinical trials.

explanation: Retrospective designs evaluate historical data, whereas prospective designs follow subjects forward in real time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h1)

question: What direction does the inquiry move in a retrospective study?

options.A: Backward from effect to cause
options.B: Sideways across multiple communities
options.C: Directly through live experimental trials
options.D: Forward from exposure to disease

explanation: The researcher identifies the outcome first and looks backward in records to find the initial exposure or cause. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why is a retrospective study considered an observational design?

options.A: The investigator actively controls the clinical environment.
options.B: The nurse must observe patients live on the hospital ward.
options.C: The researcher does not manipulate variables or assign treatments.
options.D: The study requires direct visual observation of drug administration.

explanation: Observational designs rely on recording existing events or conditions without the researcher intervening or altering treatment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h2)

question: Which retrospective design compares patients with a specific condition against those without it?

options.A: Case-control study
options.B: Randomized trial
options.C: Qualitative interview
options.D: Prospective cohort

explanation: Case-control studies select individuals with a specific outcome and compare them to controls without that outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h3)

question: A nurse researcher examines past records to compare patients with wound infections to those without infections regarding previous antibiotic use. What type of study is this?

options.A: Prospective survey
options.B: Case-control study
options.C: Experimental trial
options.D: Case report study

explanation: Comparing a group with an outcome to a group without an outcome to look at past exposures defines a case-control design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is a primary data source for conducting retrospective nursing research?

options.A: Real-time focus groups
options.B: Patient medical records
options.C: Live clinical observations
options.D: Active laboratory trials

explanation: Medical records provide the historical documentation necessary for reviewing past patient care and outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h4)

question: Why do researchers use standardized abstraction forms during retrospective data collection?

options.A: To ensure consistent data gathering across all reviewed charts
options.B: To replace the need for institutional ethical approval letters
options.C: To allow patients to update their personal health history live
options.D: To actively manipulate clinical variables during the review

explanation: Standardized forms ensure every record is evaluated using the exact same criteria, reducing data collection errors. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which benefit is a major advantage of retrospective research designs?

options.A: They require zero ethical review board approvals.
options.B: They are typically cost-effective and fast to complete.
options.C: They allow researchers to actively control clinical variables.
options.D: They completely eliminate all forms of measurement bias.

explanation: Because the data is already collected, retrospective studies save considerable time and financial resources. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h5)

question: Why are retrospective designs particularly useful when studying rare medical conditions?

options.A: Prospective follow-up takes only a few days for rare disorders.
options.B: Patients with rare conditions are easier to recruit for live interviews.
options.C: Rare diseases never appear in historical records or electronic databases.
options.D: Existing hospital archives already contain accumulated cases over many years.

explanation: Pooling historical records allows researchers to gather enough cases of rare conditions that would take too long to find prospectively. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h5)

question: What type of bias occurs when participants inaccurately remember past events?

options.A: Recall bias
options.B: Attrition bias
options.C: Selection bias
options.D: Allocation bias

explanation: Recall bias happens when study participants or staff have trouble accurately remembering details from the past. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which of the following is a major challenge when using historical nursing records for research?

options.A: Patients refuse to participate in live clinical examinations.
options.B: The researcher actively alters the past treatment given.
options.C: Incomplete charting leaves missing gaps in the required data.
options.D: Prospective follow-up timelines become too long to manage.

explanation: Past documentation is often prone to omissions, making missing data a frequent hurdle in retrospective reviews. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h6)

question: What must be secured before accessing hospital records for a retrospective study?

options.A: Immediate funding from international donors
options.B: Ethical committee approval
options.C: Verbal consent from hospital directors
options.D: Live consent from every ward nurse

explanation: Formal ethical clearance is mandatory for any research utilizing patient health records, regardless of study design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h7)

question: Why is data anonymization crucial when conducting retrospective chart reviews?

options.A: To allow researchers to contact patients directly for live interviews
options.B: To protect patient confidentiality and prevent exposure of personal health information
options.C: To speed up the statistical analysis process on hospital computers
options.D: To eliminate the possibility of missing data in the medical chart

explanation: Removing identifying details ensures patients' privacy is maintained when their historical records are analyzed. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h7)

question: What should be established first before reviewing any patient records in a study?

options.A: Final publication manuscript draft
options.B: Research question and hypothesis
options.C: Statistical software installation
options.D: Patient interview appointment times

explanation: A clear research question must guide the scope and direction of any data collection process. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h8)

question: Why are explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria necessary for selecting patient files?

options.A: To allow the researcher to alter past patient treatments
options.B: To guarantee that zero data points will ever be missing
options.C: To eliminate the need for institutional ethical clearance
options.D: To ensure only relevant and appropriate records are evaluated

explanation: Clear criteria ensure consistency and validity by defining precisely which records belong in the study population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h8)

question: What is the primary direction of time in a prospective research design?

options.A: Looking backward at past records
options.B: Moving forward into the future
options.C: Analyzing historical trends over centuries
options.D: Examining two groups at one exact moment

explanation: Prospective studies follow participants forward in time to observe outcomes as they happen. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h1)

question: How does prospective research mainly differ from retrospective research?

options.A: Prospective studies track events as they happen in real time
options.B: Retrospective studies require direct interaction with living human subjects
options.C: Retrospective studies always use larger sample sizes than prospective ones
options.D: Prospective research relies entirely on previously recorded hospital charts

explanation: The key difference is temporal orientation, where prospective designs collect fresh data as events occur. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h1)

question: When are baseline variables measured in a prospective study?

options.A: At the very beginning of the study
options.B: After the final outcome has occurred
options.C: During the data analysis phase
options.D: Only when a participant drops out

explanation: Baseline measurements establish the starting point of exposure or health status before future outcomes occur. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h2)

question: Why is it important to show that the cause happens before the effect in nursing research?

options.A: It guarantees that no participants will ever drop out
options.B: It establishes a stronger logical link for causality
options.C: It eliminates the need for any statistical testing
options.D: It reduces the financial cost of clinical trials

explanation: Showing that an exposure happens before a disease develops is a core requirement for proving cause and effect. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is a main feature of an experimental prospective clinical trial?

options.A: Investigators only observe patients without interfering
options.B: There is no comparison group used at any point
options.C: Researchers actively apply a specific intervention or treatment
options.D: Data is gathered exclusively from past hospital discharge books

explanation: Clinical trials involve an active intervention by the researcher, unlike purely observational cohort designs. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h3)

question: Which study type compares an exposed group with an unexposed group over time?

options.A: Cross-sectional prevalence survey
options.B: Case report of a single patient
options.C: Prospective cohort study
options.D: Retrospective chart review

explanation: Cohort studies follow groups based on their exposure status to see how outcomes differ over time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h3)

question: Which type of bias is mostly avoided by using a prospective design?

options.A: Measurement bias
options.B: Attrition bias
options.C: Selection bias
options.D: Recall bias

explanation: Collecting data prospectively means patients do not need to rely on memory to report past exposures. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h4)

question: Why can researchers measure variables more accurately in prospective studies?

options.A: They can plan and standardize data collection tools in advance
options.B: The computer automatically fixes any mistakes made by the nurse
options.C: Participants are always kept in a strict laboratory setting
options.D: Past records are completely ignored in favor of guesses

explanation: Advance planning allows researchers to choose precise, uniform instruments for gathering information from every participant. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h4)

question: What is attrition in the context of a prospective study?

options.A: The gradual wearing out of research equipment
options.B: A sudden decrease in study funding
options.C: The loss of data files during computer crashes
options.D: Participants dropping out over time

explanation: Attrition refers to study subjects who withdraw, move away, or are otherwise lost before the research concludes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h5)

question: Why are prospective designs difficult to use for investigating rare diseases?

options.A: They would require following an enormous number of people for many years
options.B: Ethical boards completely ban prospective work on uncommon illnesses
options.C: Statistical software cannot process data about rare health conditions
options.D: Patients with rare conditions refuse to talk to nurses in hospitals

explanation: Rare conditions occur so infrequently that a prospective cohort would need to be massive to capture enough cases. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is a practical strategy for reducing participant drop-out in a longitudinal study?

options.A: Collecting detailed contact and locator information
options.B: Stopping all communication until the final year
options.C: Keeping participants' phone numbers a secret from staff
options.D: Changing the interview questions at every single visit

explanation: Gathering thorough contact details ensures researchers can track down participants for follow-up appointments. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h6)

question: Why must data collection tools remain consistent throughout a prospective study?

options.A: To lower the cost of purchasing electronic tablets
options.B: To ensure observed changes reflect true health shifts
options.C: To satisfy hospital administrators who prefer short reports
options.D: To make sure participants do not get bored during interviews

explanation: Using uniform tools prevents measurement inconsistency from being mistaken for actual clinical progress or decline. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h6)

question: When must informed consent be obtained in a prospective study?

options.A: Before any data collection or study procedures begin
options.B: Immediately after the final data analysis is done
options.C: Only if the participant asks questions about funding
options.D: Halfway through the follow-up period

explanation: Ethical guidelines require that consent is secured before exposing participants to any research procedures. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h7)

question: What should researchers do if an interim review shows that an experimental nursing protocol causes harm?

options.A: Ignore the finding and continue as planned
options.B: Stop the study immediately
options.C: Hide the results until the study ends
options.D: Double the number of participants

explanation: Protecting human subjects from harm overrides the continuation of any research protocol. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h7)

question: How do clinical nurses use findings from prospective research studies?

options.A: To increase the cost of hospital admission fees
options.B: To replace all equipment with foreign brands
options.C: To update best practices and improve patient care
options.D: To punish staff members who make documentation errors

explanation: Evidence-based practice relies on prospective findings to guide effective bedside nursing interventions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h8)

question: Why is it important for practicing nurses to carefully evaluate prospective studies?

options.A: To determine if the research evidence is reliable enough for clinical use
options.B: To write academic textbooks for university nursing students
options.C: To avoid having to talk to patients about their care
options.D: To qualify for a promotion to hospital director

explanation: Nurses must evaluate study quality to ensure new methods are safe and effective before implementing them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T15#GNS224_U1_T15_h8)

question: What does a research population represent in a nursing study?

options.A: Only the patients admitted to the emergency ward
options.B: The group of research assistants collecting data
options.C: All citizens living in a specific local government
options.D: The entire group of people meeting study criteria

explanation: A research population includes every single individual or case that fits the predetermined specifications for a particular study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h1)

question: Why must a nurse researcher clearly define the study population early?

options.A: To guide every step of the sampling and data collection process
options.B: To reduce the total cost of purchasing hospital equipment
options.C: To eliminate the need for ethical approval from the board
options.D: To guarantee that every nurse in the hospital gets surveyed

explanation: A precise population definition determines who will be included and ensures the study remains focused and structured. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h1)

question: What is the primary difference between target and accessible populations?

options.A: The total number of male versus female patients
options.B: Whether the participants are nurses or patients
options.C: The type of statistical formula used for analysis
options.D: Feasibility and actual availability for the study

explanation: The target population is the ideal broad group, while the accessible population is the realistic subset the researcher can actually reach. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h2)

question: A researcher wants to study all midwives in Nigeria but only surveys those in Abuja. What are the Abuja midwives called?

options.A: Accessible population
options.B: Target population
options.C: Sample frame
options.D: Control group

explanation: The Abuja midwives represent the accessible population because they are the practical subgroup available from the wider national target population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h2)

question: What do inclusion criteria define in a research study?

options.A: The final sample size needed for data analysis
options.B: The conditions that disqualify people from participating
options.C: The exact statistical tests used by the researcher
options.D: The necessary traits participants must have to join

explanation: Inclusion criteria outline the exact baseline characteristics required for someone to be eligible for selection. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h3)

question: Why are exclusion criteria applied when selecting study participants?

options.A: To make sure every patient in the ward gets treated
options.B: To reduce the time spent writing the research proposal
options.C: To increase the total number of people in the hospital
options.D: To prevent confounding factors from altering the study outcomes

explanation: Exclusion criteria filter out variables that could confuse the results or endanger specific vulnerable individuals. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h3)

question: What is a sampling frame?

options.A: A summary table of inclusion and exclusion rules
options.B: A complete list of members in the accessible population
options.C: The statistical software used to analyze patient data
options.D: The physical room where interviews are conducted

explanation: A sampling frame provides the operational roster of population members from which the actual study sample is drawn. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h4)

question: A researcher selects every tenth patient entering the clinic. Which sampling method is this?

options.A: Systematic sampling
options.B: Convenience sampling
options.C: Random sampling
options.D: Stratified sampling

explanation: Choosing every nth person from a list or queue represents systematic sampling, which provides a structured way to select participants. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h4)

question: What is the main danger of using a sample size that is too small?

options.A: Excessive spending of institutional research funds
options.B: Too much data to process within a short time
options.C: Lack of statistical power to detect real effects
options.D: Unmanageable crowding in the hospital waiting room

explanation: Small sample sizes often fail to show true significant differences, leading to type II statistical errors. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h5)

question: How do researchers typically calculate the required sample size for a rigorous study?

options.A: Choosing exactly ten percent of the entire national population
options.B: Using formal power analysis and statistical formulas
options.C: Interviewing patients until the research budget is completely empty
options.D: Asking the head nurse to estimate how many files are available

explanation: Mathematical power analysis ensures the sample is large enough to yield valid and reliable scientific conclusions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h5)

question: What does generalizability mean in nursing research?

options.A: Applying study findings from a sample to a broader population
options.B: Ensuring every participant receives equal nursing care
options.C: Publishing articles in international medical journals
options.D: Generalizing the duties of nurses and doctors in a clinic

explanation: Generalizability refers to how well the results obtained from a study sample can be extended to the wider target population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why does using only volunteer participants often create sampling bias?

options.A: It automatically guarantees a 100 percent response rate
options.B: Volunteers always complete questionnaires much faster than others
options.C: Hospital management forces volunteers to alter their responses
options.D: Volunteers may possess unique traits that differ from non-volunteers

explanation: People who volunteer often have higher health motivation or different attitudes, making them unrepresentative of the entire population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T16#GNS224_U1_T16_h6)

question: What is sampling in nursing research?

options.A: Dividing research participants into experimental and control groups
options.B: Collecting blood samples from every patient in the ward
options.C: Selecting a subset of individuals to represent a larger population
options.D: Reviewing all medical records in a hospital archive

explanation: Sampling involves choosing a smaller, manageable group from a wider population to make generalized findings possible. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers study a sample instead of an entire population?

options.A: Entire populations lack the specific health conditions required for research
options.B: Ethics committees prohibit involving more than fifty patients in a study
options.C: Sampling eliminates all forms of measurement error during data collection
options.D: Studying the whole population is often impractical due to limited time and resources

explanation: Constraints like financial costs, geographic spread, and time make evaluating every member of a large population impossible. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h1)

question: The entire group of people a researcher wants to generalize study findings to is called the:

options.A: Accessible population
options.B: Control cohort
options.C: Target population
options.D: Sample group

explanation: The target population represents the ideal broader group that the research conclusions intend to apply to. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h2)

question: How does an accessible population differ from a target population?

options.A: It is the realistic subset of the target population available to the researcher
options.B: It refers strictly to the control group in experimental nursing research
options.C: It includes only patients who refuse to participate in clinical studies
options.D: It represents people living outside the geographic region of the study

explanation: Practical barriers mean researchers draw participants from the accessible segment rather than the entire global target group. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h2)

question: What do inclusion criteria define in a research study?

options.A: The reasons a participant must be removed from the ward
options.B: The financial costs approved for the research project
options.C: The specific traits a person must have to take part
options.D: The exact statistical tests used to analyze clinical data

explanation: Inclusion criteria set the baseline attributes required for someone to qualify as a study participant. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h3)

question: Why are exclusion criteria necessary for clinical nursing research?

options.A: They reduce the ethical approval waiting time to exactly one day
options.B: They ensure every single nurse in the hospital gets interviewed
options.C: They guarantee that zero participants will drop out of the study
options.D: They prevent confounding variables that could distort the study findings

explanation: Excluding certain conditions helps isolate the specific intervention or variable being investigated without interference. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h3)

question: Which sampling method gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection?

options.A: Purposive sampling
options.B: Convenience sampling
options.C: Snowball sampling
options.D: Probability sampling

explanation: Random selection is the defining feature of probability sampling techniques. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h4)

question: A researcher divides a hospital nursing staff into junior, mid-level, and senior cadres, then draws random names from each. What is this technique?

options.A: Stratified random sampling
options.B: Simple random sampling
options.C: Quota sampling
options.D: Convenience sampling

explanation: Dividing the population into subgroups (strata) and randomly selecting from each ensures representation across all groups. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h4)

question: Selecting patients who walk into the outpatient clinic simply because they are easy to reach is an example of:

options.A: Systematic sampling
options.B: Random sampling
options.C: Convenience sampling
options.D: Stratified sampling

explanation: Convenience sampling relies on readily available subjects rather than random selection. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h5)

question: When is purposive sampling most appropriate to use in nursing studies?

options.A: When studying a specific group of experts with unique clinical experiences
options.B: When there is an unlimited budget and plenty of time for random draws
options.C: When every patient in the country has an equal chance of being selected
options.D: When the researcher wants to generalize results to the entire global population

explanation: Purposive sampling targets specific individuals who can provide deep, relevant insight into the phenomenon under study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h5)

question: What does statistical power measure in nursing research?

options.A: The financial backing provided by the hospital management board
options.B: The speed at which data collectors enter information into software
options.C: The ability of a study to detect a real effect when it exists
options.D: The physical strength required by nurses to lift heavy equipment

explanation: Statistical power ensures the study is large enough to avoid missing genuine clinical findings. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h6)

question: Why is recruiting a larger sample size than mathematically required often necessary in clinical trials?

options.A: To guarantee that every participant receives an experimental drug
options.B: To ensure that no statistical calculations are ever required during analysis
options.C: To eliminate the need for inclusion and exclusion criteria entirely
options.D: To account for participants who drop out or withdraw before the study ends

explanation: Attrition happens when participants leave a study, so researchers recruit extra subjects to maintain adequate final sample size. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is sampling bias in research?

options.A: An error caused by broken laboratory equipment during specimen collection
options.B: The mathematical formula used to calculate statistical significance
options.C: A systematic flaw where certain population members are favored for inclusion
options.D: The natural random difference between a sample and its parent population

explanation: Sampling bias skews results because the sample is not truly representative of the population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h7)

question: Which factor primarily helps to reduce natural sampling error in a quantitative study?

options.A: Increasing the overall sample size
options.B: Removing statistical power calculations
options.C: Narrowing down the inclusion criteria to one person
options.D: Using a non-probability convenience method

explanation: Larger samples better reflect the true characteristics of the population, thereby reducing random sampling error. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the primary reason researchers use a sample instead of an entire population?

options.A: Sampling eliminates all forms of research bias completely
options.B: Ethical boards forbid studying large groups of patients
options.C: Data analysis is easier when fewer variables are collected
options.D: Resource and time constraints make studying everyone impossible

explanation: Studying an entire population requires too much time, money, and logistics, making a smaller sample necessary. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h1)

question: A good sample in nursing research must possess which essential quality?

options.A: It must include every single member of the hospital ward
options.B: It must consist entirely of patients with severe illnesses
options.C: It must represent the wider target population accurately
options.D: It must avoid using any statistical tests for analysis

explanation: Representativeness ensures that conclusions drawn from the study participants apply to the broader patient group. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h1)

question: What name is given to the complete list of all elements in the accessible population?

options.A: Sampling frame
options.B: Pilot registry
options.C: Target demographic
options.D: Variable index

explanation: The sampling frame serves as the practical operational list from which study participants are chosen. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T18#GNS224_U1_T18_h2)

question: A researcher studies nurses in Lagos State University Teaching Hospital by using the current hospital payroll register. What does the payroll register represent?

options.A: The sample group
options.B: The target population
options.C: The exclusion criteria
options.D: The sampling frame
