options.A: It guarantees that patients will not experience side effects.
options.B: It removes the need for any statistical software.
options.C: It replaces the need for an institutional ethics review.
options.D: It guides the logical collection and analysis of data.

explanation: A clear design serves as a roadmap to ensure variables are measured accurately and research questions are answered reliably. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h1)

question: The process of testing a general theory by observing specific instances is called what?

options.A: Phenomenology
options.B: Deductive reasoning
options.C: Inductive reasoning
options.D: Ethnography

explanation: Deductive reasoning starts with a broad theory and tests it through specific observations and data collection. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h2)

question: Maintaining strict control over study conditions primarily helps to achieve what outcome?

options.A: Increasing the length of the research report
options.B: Ensuring participants enjoy the intervention
options.C: Minimizing the effect of confounding variables
options.D: Eliminating the need for informed consent

explanation: Control measures keep outside factors from skewing the results, ensuring that changes in the dependent variable are truly due to the intervention. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which component is strictly required in a true experimental design?

options.A: Open-ended questionnaires
options.B: Historical controls
options.C: Qualitative interviews
options.D: Random assignment

explanation: Random assignment ensures that every participant has an equal chance of being in the treatment or control group, balancing out baseline differences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h3)

question: A researcher wants to prove that a new nursing protocol directly causes a drop in falls. Which design must be chosen?

options.A: Phenomenological design
options.B: Case study design
options.C: Experimental design
options.D: Descriptive design

explanation: Only experimental designs provide the high level of control and manipulation necessary to establish definitive cause-and-effect relationships. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h3)

question: A quasi-experimental study differs from a true experiment mainly because it lacks what feature?

options.A: An independent variable
options.B: Random assignment
options.C: Data collection tools
options.D: A research question

explanation: Quasi-experiments manipulate the independent variable and use comparison groups, but they typically use pre-existing groups instead of random assignment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h4)

question: When is a quasi-experimental design preferred over a true experimental design in a hospital?

options.A: When there is no need to compare two different groups of people.
options.B: When proving absolute causation is the absolute top priority.
options.C: When the researcher wants to avoid collecting any numerical data.
options.D: When randomly assigning patients to specific units is completely impractical.

explanation: Clinical realities often prevent random assignment, making quasi-experimental designs a practical and ethical alternative for nursing research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is a defining feature of non-experimental research designs?

options.A: Active treatment of the control group
options.B: Mandatory random assignment
options.C: Creation of artificial laboratory conditions
options.D: Absence of variable manipulation

explanation: Non-experimental research observes phenomena naturally without introducing any interventions or changing the study environment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h5)

question: A nurse studies the relationship between years of shift work and chronic fatigue scores. Which design fits best?

options.A: True experimental design
options.B: Experimental intervention design
options.C: Randomized controlled trial
options.D: Correlational design

explanation: Correlational designs are used when a researcher wants to examine the relationship or association between two or more existing variables without manipulating them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h5)

question: The outcome variable that changes in response to an intervention is called what?

options.A: Independent variable
options.B: Dependent variable
options.C: Demographic variable
options.D: Extraneous variable

explanation: The dependent variable represents the effect or outcome that the researcher is trying to predict or measure. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why is an operational definition essential for variables in a quantitative study?

options.A: It replaces the need for statistical tests during data analysis.
options.B: It removes all potential bias from the independent variable entirely.
options.C: It turns a qualitative narrative study into a purely historical review.
options.D: It clearly specifies how a variable will be measured and observed.

explanation: Operational definitions provide explicit instructions on how to measure abstract concepts so data collection remains consistent and reliable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h6)

question: The consistency and stability of a research measurement tool over time is known as:

options.A: Objectivity
options.B: Generalizability
options.C: Reliability
options.D: Validity

explanation: Reliability means that if you repeat the measurement under the same conditions, you will get the same or very similar results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h7)

question: A blood pressure cuff is broken and gives readings that are consistently 20 points too high. This tool is best described as having:

options.A: Reliability but poor validity
options.B: High validity and high reliability
options.C: Neither reliability nor validity
options.D: Complete lack of any clinical utility

explanation: The tool consistently gives the same incorrect number, meaning it is reliable in its consistency, but invalid because it fails to show the true blood pressure. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is required before a patient can participate in a quantitative clinical study?

options.A: A personal referral
options.B: Hospital admission
options.C: Informed consent
options.D: Financial compensation

explanation: Informed consent ensures participants understand the study's risks and benefits and agree to join voluntarily. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h8)

question: Why must a nurse researcher submit their quantitative proposal to an ethics committee?

options.A: To secure funding for laboratory equipment and supplies.
options.B: To speed up the final publication process in medical journals.
options.C: To safeguard the rights and welfare of human participants.
options.D: To guarantee that the study will achieve statistical significance.

explanation: Ethics committees independently review protocols to ensure participants are protected from undue harm, exploitation, or coercion. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h8)

question: What is the main goal of qualitative research in nursing?

options.A: Understanding human experiences and meanings
options.B: Measuring statistical frequency of diseases
options.C: Establishing cause and effect through trials
options.D: Calculating precise drug dosage responses

explanation: Qualitative research explores subjective human experiences rather than counting numerical data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which of these is a good research question for a qualitative nursing study?

options.A: What is the average blood pressure after medication
options.B: How mothers cope with sickle cell crises at home
options.C: What percentage of patients develop pressure ulcers
options.D: How many hours nurses spend on documentation daily

explanation: Qualitative questions explore experiences and coping mechanisms rather than measuring numerical variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which study design looks specifically at the lived experiences of individuals?

options.A: Phenomenology
options.B: Ethnography
options.C: Historical research
options.D: Grounded theory

explanation: Phenomenological research centers entirely on understanding the lived subjective experiences of people. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h2)

question: A researcher wants to learn about the health practices of Fulani pastoralists by living among them. Which design is best?

options.A: Phenomenology
options.B: Ethnography
options.C: Clinical trial
options.D: Grounded theory

explanation: Ethnographic studies involve cultural immersion to understand group behaviors and societal norms from within. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h2)

question: What sampling method chooses participants on purpose based on specific study needs?

options.A: Random sampling
options.B: Cluster sampling
options.C: Stratified sampling
options.D: Purposive sampling

explanation: Purposive sampling deliberately targets individuals who can provide rich, relevant information about the research topic. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h3)

question: Theoretical sampling is most often used in which type of qualitative study?

options.A: Ethnography
options.B: Case study
options.C: Grounded theory
options.D: Phenomenology

explanation: Theoretical sampling directs further data collection based on evolving concepts during data analysis in grounded theory studies. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h3)

question: Why do qualitative interviews use open-ended questions?

options.A: To generate numerical data for statistical testing
options.B: To keep the interview strictly under ten minutes
options.C: To restrict answers to simple yes or no responses
options.D: To allow participants to share detailed personal accounts

explanation: Open-ended questions encourage expansive narratives rather than restricted or quantifiable answers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h4)

question: A researcher wants to watch how nurses naturally interact at a triage desk. Which method works best?

options.A: Focus group
options.B: Observation
options.C: Randomized trial
options.D: Survey questionnaire

explanation: Observation allows researchers to witness real-world behaviors and interactions directly in their natural setting. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which quality check in qualitative research matches internal validity in quantitative studies?

options.A: Dependability
options.B: Credibility
options.C: Transferability
options.D: Confirmability

explanation: Credibility establishes whether the research findings accurately reflect the participants' original meanings and experiences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h5)

question: How do qualitative researchers show that their study results are confirmable?

options.A: By avoiding any interaction with study participants
options.B: By ensuring every participant gives the exact same answer
options.C: By calculating statistical p-values from interview transcripts
options.D: By maintaining an audit trail of data analysis steps

explanation: An audit trail documents the analytical steps taken, proving the results derive from data rather than researcher bias. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the usual first step before qualitative data analysis begins?

options.A: Destroying original field notes immediately
options.B: Publishing the final research manuscript
options.C: Transcribing audio recordings verbatim
options.D: Calculating numerical averages of codes

explanation: Verbatim transcription converts spoken interviews into written text required for coding and thematic analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h6)

question: During qualitative data analysis, what step comes right after initial coding of text?

options.A: Applying statistical formulas to test hypotheses
options.B: Discarding data that does not fit the researcher's view
options.C: Converting all written words into numerical percentages
options.D: Grouping similar codes into broader categories and themes

explanation: Coders organize individual codes into overarching categories and themes to synthesize the core meanings in the data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is essential when publishing direct quotes from qualitative interviews?

options.A: Protecting participant anonymity and confidentiality
options.B: Translating all quotes into medical terminology
options.C: Obtaining permission from hospital board members first
options.D: Including the participant's full residential address

explanation: Researchers must scrub identifiable details to protect participant privacy when sharing qualitative data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why can the dual role of nurse-researcher be an ethical concern in qualitative studies?

options.A: Nursing licenses do not permit qualitative data collection
options.B: Researchers cannot use audio recorders in clinical settings
options.C: Patients will refuse to take their prescribed medications
options.D: Participants may feel pressured to share because of the nurse's authority

explanation: The clinical authority of a nurse can create coercion, making patients feel they must participate in the study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h7)

question: What does a research paradigm represent in nursing studies?

options.A: A hospital management rule
options.B: A specific statistical formula
options.C: A clinical treatment protocol
options.D: A worldview and belief system

explanation: A research paradigm represents the fundamental worldview and belief system that guides how a researcher views and studies reality. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do nursing students learn about different research paradigms?

options.A: To properly appraise published studies and select methods
options.B: To avoid ever having to use statistical software
options.C: To replace standard hospital operating procedures
options.D: To diagnose complex patient illnesses accurately

explanation: Knowing research paradigms helps nurses critically evaluate published literature and choose appropriate study designs for clinical questions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h1)

question: What is the primary type of data collected in quantitative research?

options.A: Numerical data
options.B: Field diary notes
options.C: Open narratives
options.D: Audio recordings

explanation: Quantitative research fundamentally relies on numbers and numerical measurements to quantify variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is a major purpose of using a quantitative design in a nursing study?

options.A: Exploring deep emotional feelings of a single patient
options.B: Describing historical events in healthcare
options.C: Recording daily ward gossip without structure
options.D: Testing specific hypotheses and generalizing findings

explanation: Quantitative designs aim to test predictions and apply results to a broader population through statistical analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h2)

question: What type of data is central to qualitative research designs?

options.A: Blood pressure readings
options.B: Height and weight measurements
options.C: Words and narratives
options.D: Laboratory test scores

explanation: Qualitative research gathers rich verbal data such as interviews, transcripts, and field notes rather than numerical measurements. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h3)

question: When is a qualitative research design most appropriate for a nursing study?

options.A: When exploring the lived experience of living with chronic illness
options.B: When comparing blood sugar levels before and after exercise
options.C: When calculating the average length of hospital stay
options.D: When measuring the exact dosage of a medication

explanation: Qualitative designs excel at capturing subjective human experiences and deep personal meanings that numbers cannot express. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h3)

question: How does the view of reality (ontology) differ between quantitative and qualitative research?

options.A: Quantitative avoids statistics, while qualitative uses complex formulas
options.B: Quantitative studies groups, while qualitative studies animals
options.C: Quantitative relies on words, while qualitative relies purely on blood tests
options.D: Quantitative assumes one objective reality, while qualitative assumes multiple realities

explanation: Quantitative research views truth as fixed and measurable, whereas qualitative research views reality as subjective and shaped by human experience. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h4)

question: How does a quantitative researcher approach objectivity in a study?

options.A: Remaining detached and objective from the study participants
options.B: Changing the research question based on daily feelings
options.C: Relying entirely on personal intuition and beliefs
options.D: Immersing fully in the daily lives of the patients

explanation: Quantitative researchers maintain distance to prevent bias and ensure objective measurement of variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which data collection method is most characteristic of qualitative nursing studies?

options.A: Automated blood pressure cuffs
options.B: Standardized multiple-choice exams
options.C: Rigid computerized lab analyzers
options.D: In-depth open-ended interviews

explanation: Qualitative research uses unstructured or semi-structured interviews to let participants share their stories in detail. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h5)

question: Why are structured questionnaires commonly used in quantitative research?

options.A: To encourage patients to share personal life stories without limits
options.B: To collect standardized numerical data that can be easily analyzed
options.C: To allow the interviewer to change questions based on mood
options.D: To avoid gathering any measurable information from patients

explanation: Structured tools ensure every participant answers the same questions in the same way, yielding uniform data for statistical analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h5)

question: What technique is commonly used to analyze qualitative textual data?

options.A: Chi-square testing
options.B: Thematic coding and categorization
options.C: Analysis of variance calculations
options.D: Linear regression modeling

explanation: Qualitative data is broken down into codes and grouped into broader themes to interpret meaning from text. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of inferential statistics in quantitative data analysis?

options.A: To summarize the basic age and gender of study participants
options.B: To translate foreign patient records into English
options.C: To organize written interview transcripts into paragraphs
options.D: To draw conclusions about a larger population based on sample data

explanation: Inferential statistics help researchers test hypotheses and generalize findings from a sample to the wider population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h6)

question: What two core criteria are used to evaluate rigor in quantitative studies?

options.A: Subjectivity and intuition
options.B: Credibility and transferability
options.C: Validity and reliability
options.D: Flexibility and emotion

explanation: Quantitative research measures quality using validity (accuracy) and reliability (consistency). [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h7)

question: Which term describes trustworthiness in qualitative research when checking if findings reflect participants' real views?

options.A: Generalizability
options.B: Probability
options.C: Reliability
options.D: Credibility

explanation: Credibility in qualitative research ensures the study accurately represents the actual perspectives of the participants. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h7)

question: A nurse wants to know if a new wound dressing heals ulcers faster than the standard dressing. Which research design is best suited?

options.A: Ethnographic observation study
options.B: Qualitative phenomenological design
options.C: Historical biographical study
options.D: Quantitative experimental design

explanation: Comparing healing times and rates requires numerical measurement and hypothesis testing, which is quantitative work. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h8)

question: When is a mixed-methods research design most useful in nursing practice?

options.A: When only financial cost matters to the hospital
options.B: When combining numerical outcomes with deep patient perspectives
options.C: When there is no clinical question to investigate
options.D: When the researcher wants to avoid doing any data analysis

explanation: Mixed-methods research integrates both quantitative and qualitative data to give a complete picture of a complex clinical issue. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of an experimental research design?

options.A: To explore new concepts through interviews
options.B: To establish cause-and-effect relationships
options.C: To observe subjects without any interference
options.D: To describe the characteristics of a population

explanation: Experimental designs actively manipulate variables to determine if one causes a change in another. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why does experimental research hold a higher rank than descriptive studies in evidence-based practice?

options.A: It requires no ethical committee approval
options.B: It relies entirely on patient opinions
options.C: It proves direct causation rather than mere association
options.D: It is always cheaper and faster to complete

explanation: Intervention and control allow researchers to link an action directly to an outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h1)

question: Random assignment in an experiment is done primarily to achieve what goal?

options.A: Make patients follow their prescribed treatment
options.B: Hide the true hypothesis from the participants
options.C: Spread confounding traits evenly across study groups
options.D: Ensure the sample size is as large as possible

explanation: Randomization neutralizes baseline differences so groups start out as equal as possible. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h2)

question: What happens to a study if the researcher fails to maintain proper control over extraneous factors?

options.A: Participants will instantly drop out of the trial
options.B: The institutional review board will automatically dismiss the paper
options.C: The independent variable stops existing altogether
options.D: Alternative explanations for the outcome cannot be ruled out

explanation: Without control, outside factors might be causing the measured changes instead of the intervention. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which design lacks both random assignment and a control group?

options.A: Quasi-experimental design
options.B: Pre-experimental design
options.C: True experimental design
options.D: Randomized controlled trial

explanation: Pre-experimental designs offer very weak control and are typically used for quick pilot checks. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h3)

question: When is a nurse researcher most likely to choose a quasi-experimental design over a true experiment?

options.A: When random assignment of patients to wards is impossible
options.B: When proving absolute causation is the only goal
options.C: When funding is completely unlimited and abundant
options.D: When no human participants are involved in the study

explanation: Clinical realities often require using pre-existing groups, making quasi-experimental methods necessary. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h3)

question: The variable that measures the final outcome or effect in an experiment is called what?

options.A: Dependent variable
options.B: Confounding variable
options.C: Extraneous variable
options.D: Independent variable

explanation: The dependent variable relies on or responds to the changes made by the independent variable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h4)

question: A researcher notices room temperature is affecting patient recovery rates during a drug trial. What is room temperature classified as?

options.A: Independent variable
options.B: Dependent variable
options.C: Random variable
options.D: Extraneous variable

explanation: Any outside factor that influences the dependent variable without being part of the planned study is an extraneous variable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h4)

question: What does internal validity evaluate in a research study?

options.A: Whether the results apply to patients in other hospitals
options.B: How many nurses volunteered to help with the data collection
options.C: Whether the intervention truly caused the observed outcome
options.D: How well the laboratory equipment was calibrated

explanation: Internal validity guards against alternative explanations for the study results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h5)

question: A study is conducted using only young, healthy male athletes in one clinic. Which type of validity is most severely threatened?

options.A: Construct validity
options.B: External validity
options.C: Internal validity
options.D: Statistical validity

explanation: Narrow sample demographics limit the ability to generalize findings to the broader public. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h5)

question: What must a nurse researcher secure before any human participant enters an experimental study?

options.A: A commercial sponsor for drug supplies
options.B: Complete exemption from data collection rules
options.C: Ethical approval from a review board
options.D: Immediate publication in a foreign journal

explanation: Institutional review board approval is mandatory to protect human subjects from harm. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h6)

question: Why is baseline data collection necessary before administering an experimental treatment?

options.A: To help recruit more patients into the hospital ward
options.B: To ensure the nurses get paid for their research time
options.C: To replace the need for a statistical data analysis plan
options.D: To prove that both study groups start from a similar place

explanation: Baseline measurements verify that randomization worked and groups are comparable before treatment begins. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h6)

question: What document guarantees that a patient knows the risks and benefits of joining a study?

options.A: Nursing care plan sheet
options.B: Informed consent form
options.C: Patient financial receipt
options.D: Hospital discharge summary

explanation: Informed consent documents ensure voluntary participation based on full disclosure of study details. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h7)

question: Why is withholding a clearly life-saving treatment from a control group considered ethically challenging?

options.A: It automatically invalidates all statistical software outputs
options.B: It violates the duty to protect patient well-being
options.C: It causes the independent variable to disappear
options.D: It makes the research paper too expensive to print

explanation: Researchers have an ethical obligation to prioritize patient safety and welfare above study completion. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is a major limitation of strict experimental designs in clinical practice?

options.A: They often use artificial samples that do not mirror messy real-world wards
options.B: They prevent nurses from ever reading medical journals
options.C: They are universally cheaper than any other type of research
options.D: They completely eliminate the need for statistical calculations

explanation: Controlled environments remove real-world variables, making direct translation to chaotic clinical floors challenging. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h8)

question: How do completed experimental studies directly influence everyday nursing practice?

options.A: By dictating how many nurses must work each shift on a ward
options.B: By providing high-level evidence to update hospital clinical guidelines
options.C: By removing all paperwork requirements from patient admissions
options.D: By replacing doctors in emergency diagnostic decision-making

explanation: Strong trial outcomes form the backbone of evidence-based protocols used at the bedside. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h8)

question: What is the main feature of a non-experimental research design?

options.A: Absence of researcher manipulation of the independent variable
options.B: Controlled laboratory setting for all observations
options.C: Random assignment of patients to treatment groups
options.D: Deliberate introduction of a clinical intervention

explanation: Non-experimental studies observe phenomena naturally without the researcher altering or manipulating any variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers often choose non-experimental designs in clinical practice?

options.A: These designs always prove direct cause and effect relationships
options.B: Many clinical variables cannot ethically or practically be manipulated
options.C: Data collection takes less than twenty-four hours to complete
options.D: Hospital management requires non-experimental data for funding

explanation: Ethical constraints often prevent researchers from altering patient conditions, making observation the only viable option. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is the main goal of a descriptive research design?

options.A: Compare two active nursing interventions against each other
options.B: Determine the direct cause of a specific clinical symptom
options.C: Accurately characterize a phenomenon or patient population
options.D: Manipulate environmental factors to observe patient recovery

explanation: Descriptive studies focus on documenting and summarizing existing characteristics without testing causal links. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h2)

question: A nurse surveys postpartum mothers to find out the exact percentage who practice exclusive breastfeeding. What type of study is this?

options.A: Causal-comparative
options.B: Descriptive
options.C: Correlational
options.D: Experimental

explanation: Measuring the frequency of a behavior in a population without testing relationships fits a descriptive design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h2)

question: What does a correlation coefficient of zero indicate?

options.A: A perfect positive linear relationship
options.B: A strong negative association between factors
options.C: No relationship between the two variables
options.D: An error in the data collection process

explanation: A coefficient of zero means the variables do not vary together in any predictable linear pattern. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h3)

question: A research finding shows that higher levels of patient anxiety are linked to higher reported pain scores. What type of correlation is this?

options.A: Inverse correlation
options.B: Zero correlation
options.C: Negative correlation
options.D: Positive correlation

explanation: When both variables increase together, the relationship is classified as a positive correlation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h3)

question: When is an ex post facto research design used by nurses?

options.A: When the researcher actively manipulates patient medication doses
options.B: When testing a brand new drug in a randomized clinical trial
options.C: When conducting real-time observation of emergency room triage
options.D: When the independent variable has already occurred naturally

explanation: Ex post facto designs study groups that already differ on an independent variable due to past events. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why is it difficult to show cause and effect in an ex post facto study?

options.A: Alternative explanations and confounding variables cannot be fully ruled out
options.B: Ethical boards prohibit publishing retrospective clinical findings
options.C: Patients usually refuse to share accurate details about their past medical history
options.D: The sample size is always too small to calculate statistical significance

explanation: Without random assignment and manipulation, other hidden factors could explain the observed differences between groups. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is the main feature of a cross-sectional study?

options.A: Data is gathered at a single point in time
options.B: Participants are followed over a period of many years
options.C: The researcher actively introduces a new clinical therapy
options.D: Measurements are repeated weekly for at least six months

explanation: Cross-sectional designs provide a snapshot of a population at one specific moment without follow-up. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which challenge is most common in longitudinal research designs?

options.A: Inability to measure more than one variable at the baseline
options.B: Extremely high costs of analyzing single snapshot surveys
options.C: Participants dropping out or being lost to follow-up over time
options.D: Total lack of ethical oversight for long-term patient contact

explanation: Attrition is a major threat to longitudinal studies because keeping track of the same cohort over time is difficult. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which of the following is a main advantage of non-experimental research?

options.A: Elimination of bias during data collection and analysis
options.B: High external validity due to real-world setting observation
options.C: Definitive proof of cause and effect relationships
options.D: Complete control over all extraneous confounding variables

explanation: Observing phenomena in natural environments makes the findings easier to generalize to everyday clinical practice. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is a major weakness when relying only on non-experimental data for clinical guidelines?

options.A: Excessive use of expensive laboratory equipment and supplies
options.B: Failure to obtain ethical approval from institutional review boards
options.C: Inability to confirm that the independent variable caused the outcome
options.D: Unwillingness of patients to participate in observational surveys

explanation: Without experimental control, researchers cannot rule out alternative reasons for observed outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the main goal of descriptive research?

options.A: To accurately portray characteristics of a population
options.B: To manipulate independent variables in a lab
options.C: To test new pharmaceutical drugs on patients
options.D: To prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship

explanation: Descriptive research focuses on observing and documenting characteristics of a group or situation without changing anything. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h1)

question: A nurse wants to know the exact breakdown of hypertension stages in a rural clinic. Which design should be used?

options.A: Randomized controlled trial
options.B: Quasi-experimental design
options.C: Descriptive research design
options.D: True experimental design

explanation: Descriptive designs map out the current distribution of conditions or traits within a specific group. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which feature is a key characteristic of descriptive research?

options.A: Random assignment of subjects to trial arms
options.B: Active intervention by the clinical investigator
options.C: Strict control of environmental confounding factors
options.D: Absence of variable manipulation by the researcher

explanation: Researchers measure variables exactly as they occur in nature during descriptive studies without interfering. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h2)

question: Why do nurse researchers often start with a descriptive study before planning an experiment?

options.A: To reduce the total financial cost of clinical trials
options.B: To identify baseline patterns and generate hypotheses
options.C: To eliminate the need for ethical committee approval
options.D: To prove definitively that one intervention cures a disease

explanation: Descriptive studies uncover current trends and gaps, which helps form the foundation for later experimental testing. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h2)

question: What type of descriptive design takes an in-depth look at a single clinical case or unit?

options.A: Cohort study
options.B: Meta-analysis
options.C: Clinical trial
options.D: Case study

explanation: A case study focuses deeply on one specific subject, patient, or unique clinical situation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h3)

question: A researcher gives questionnaires to 500 nursing students to check stress levels. What kind of design is this?

options.A: Case-control study
options.B: Experimental research
options.C: Clinical audit
options.D: Survey research

explanation: Using questionnaires to gather self-reported data from a large group is a classic example of survey research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h3)

question: What tool is best for directly observing clinical behaviors?

options.A: Checklists and rating scales
options.B: Laboratory blood analyzers
options.C: Double-blinded pill dispensers
options.D: Randomized assignment software

explanation: Checklists allow observers to systematically record specific actions as they happen in real-time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h4)

question: A nurse wants to check patient satisfaction on a surgical ward. Which tool works best?

options.A: An animal laboratory model
options.B: A structured questionnaire
options.C: A laboratory biopsy report
options.D: A double-blind drug trial

explanation: Questionnaires efficiently gather self-reported feedback about satisfaction from a broad group of patients. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is the very first step when doing a descriptive research study?

options.A: Distributing incentive payments
options.B: Identifying the research problem
options.C: Analyzing the collected data
options.D: Publishing the final journal article

explanation: Every research journey begins by clearly defining the problem or question you want to explore. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why is defining the target population important before collecting data in a descriptive study?

options.A: It guarantees a statistically significant cause-and-effect link
options.B: It eliminates all possible sources of measurement bias
options.C: It ensures the findings accurately represent the group being studied
options.D: It forces the researcher to use experimental manipulation

explanation: Clear population boundaries ensure that the descriptive data collected applies directly to the intended group. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h5)

question: Which statistical measure shows the spread or dispersion of data scores?

options.A: Median middle score
options.B: Standard deviation
options.C: Mode frequent entry
options.D: Mean average value

explanation: Standard deviation measures how far individual data points deviate from the central average. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h6)

question: Why are inferential statistics usually avoided as the main analysis in pure descriptive research?

options.A: Inferential statistics require active drug administration to subjects
options.B: Descriptive studies do not test experimental hypotheses between variables
options.C: Calculations for percentages are mathematically impossible to compute
options.D: Computers cannot process numbers gathered from observational checklists

explanation: Descriptive studies map current status rather than testing cause-and-effect relationships, making descriptive statistics enough. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is a major limitation of descriptive research designs?

options.A: Inability to establish cause-and-effect relationships
options.B: Mandatory requirement for complex surgical interventions
options.C: Excessive financial cost required for laboratory setups
options.D: Extreme difficulty in finding any willing human subjects

explanation: Because variables are only observed and not manipulated, descriptive research cannot prove that one thing causes another. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h7)

question: Which issue can weaken the reliability of survey-based descriptive research?

options.A: Random assignment errors made by the researcher
options.B: Interference caused by surgical drug administration
options.C: Response bias from participants answering to look good
options.D: Excessive control over the natural environment

explanation: Self-reported surveys often suffer when participants alter answers to appear more favorable or please the researcher. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h7)

question: A head nurse tracks monthly rates of pressure ulcers across wards. What is this an example of?

options.A: Performing a randomized controlled trial on a new wound dressing
options.B: Testing a surgical intervention for wound closure
options.C: Using descriptive research to monitor clinical quality indicators
options.D: Manipulating patient positioning schedules experimentally

explanation: Tracking rates of clinical occurrences like pressure ulcers is a direct application of descriptive research in quality improvement. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h8)

question: How do descriptive studies help nurse managers in hospital administration?

options.A: By proving which specific nurse caused a medication error
options.B: By eliminating the need for hospital budget approvals
options.C: By replacing all clinical judgment with automated computer algorithms
options.D: By providing data on staffing needs and patient demographics for planning

explanation: Descriptive profiles of patient loads and staff workloads help managers make informed administrative decisions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h8)

question: What does research data primarily represent in nursing studies?

options.A: Information, measurements, or observations
options.B: Personal opinions of the hospital staff
options.C: Theoretical concepts without observation
options.D: Financial budgets for clinical wards

explanation: Research data consists of concrete pieces of information and observations gathered during a study to evaluate clinical questions. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why must nurses be able to recognize different types of research data?

options.A: To properly evaluate the validity of clinical studies
options.B: To diagnose complex medical diseases independently
options.C: To manage the daily human resource schedule
options.D: To write hospital billing invoices for patient care

explanation: Understanding data helps nurses appraise research evidence so they can safely apply valid findings to patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h1)

question: A patient's daily fluid intake measured in millilitres is an example of what data type?

options.A: Qualitative data
options.B: Quantitative data
options.C: Secondary data
options.D: Nominal data

explanation: Fluid intake is measured in numbers and quantities, which defines quantitative data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h2)

question: A descriptive interview transcript detailing a mother's coping experience represents which form of data?

options.A: Qualitative data
options.B: Quantitative data
options.C: Ratio data
options.D: Nominal data

explanation: Narrative descriptions and words capturing human experiences constitute qualitative data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which level of measurement classifies data into categories that have a distinct logical order?

options.A: Nominal
options.B: Interval
options.C: Ordinal
options.D: Ratio

explanation: Ordinal data places observations into ranked categories, such as mild, moderate, or severe pain. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h3)

question: A nurse records a patient's exact blood potassium level as 4.2 mmol/L. What level of measurement is this?

options.A: Ratio
options.B: Ordinal
options.C: Nominal
options.D: Interval

explanation: Measurements with equal intervals and an absolute true zero point, where zero means complete absence of the property, are ratio data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the defining feature of primary research data?

options.A: Collected firsthand for the current specific study
options.B: Analyzed using qualitative interview transcripts
options.C: Extracted from old hospital admission registers
options.D: Obtained exclusively from government census reports

explanation: Primary data is gathered directly by the researcher to answer the specific research question at hand. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h4)

question: A nurse researcher reviewing past patient folders in the records department is using which data source?

options.A: Ordinal data
options.B: Secondary data
options.C: Nominal data
options.D: Primary data

explanation: Using records or datasets originally compiled by others for past care or different studies constitutes secondary data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h4)

question: What does an independent variable represent in a nursing research study?

options.A: The final measured outcome or clinical effect
options.B: The demographic category of the nursing staff
options.C: The presumed cause or experimental intervention
options.D: The random error found in laboratory tests

explanation: The independent variable is manipulated or observed as the cause or predictor affecting the outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why can the same clinical factor act as an independent variable in one study and a dependent variable in another?

options.A: Researchers change data types randomly during statistical analysis
options.B: Nominal data automatically converts into ratio measurements over time
options.C: Its classification depends entirely on the specific research question
options.D: Secondary data sources lack the structure of primary collections

explanation: A variable's role is not fixed; it depends on what the researcher is investigating as the cause versus the effect. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of data screening before statistical analysis?

options.A: To check for entry errors, missing values, and outliers
options.B: To change secondary research sources into primary data
options.C: To convert all qualitative notes into quantitative numbers
options.D: To eliminate the need for institutional ethical approval

explanation: Data screening identifies mistakes, missing entries, and unrealistic outliers that could ruin the analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h6)

question: A researcher notices a patient's temperature recorded as 450 degrees Celsius on a data sheet. What does this represent?

options.A: A secondary data source from hospital archives
options.B: An impossible data entry error requiring correction
options.C: A normal ratio measurement of high fever
options.D: An acceptable qualitative observation note

explanation: Values outside biological possibility indicate data entry mistakes that must be cleaned before analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h6)

question: In a research data table, what does a single row usually stand for?

options.A: A specific research hypothesis
options.B: The statistical test applied
options.C: An individual study participant
options.D: A measured clinical variable

explanation: Rows in a data table stand for individual subjects, while columns stand for the specific variables you measured. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is it important to organize research data right after collecting it?

options.A: It eliminates the need for patient consent forms
options.B: It guarantees statistically significant study findings
options.C: It reduces the total number of required participants
options.D: It prevents errors during subsequent statistical analysis

explanation: Arranging your data early helps you spot and fix mistakes before you start running calculations. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which measurement scale sorts data into categories that do not have any numerical order?

options.A: Ordinal scale
options.B: Interval scale
options.C: Nominal scale
options.D: Ratio scale

explanation: Nominal data simply names or labels categories without ranking them, such as blood groups or gender. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h2)

question: A nurse records a patient's temperature in Celsius. Which measurement scale is this?

options.A: Ordinal scale
options.B: Ratio scale
options.C: Nominal scale
options.D: Interval scale

explanation: Celsius temperatures have equal units between numbers, but zero does not mean a complete absence of heat, making it interval data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the main reason for coding text-based or qualitative responses in research?

options.A: To assign numerical values for software analysis
options.B: To eliminate missing values from the data set
options.C: To hide the true identity of study subjects
options.D: To convert interval data into nominal scales

explanation: Coding turns descriptive answers into numbers so computer software can read and calculate them. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why must you clean your data before running statistical tests?

options.A: It automatically increases the statistical power of the study
options.B: It replaces the need for informed consent documents
options.C: It identifies entry mistakes and illogical values that distort results
options.D: It converts non-parametric data into parametric distributions

explanation: Data cleaning catches typos and impossible values so they do not ruin your final results. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h3)

question: What does relative frequency show in a distribution table?

options.A: The total number of participants in the study
options.B: The percentage or proportion of a specific category
options.C: The difference between maximum and minimum values
options.D: The cumulative sum of all raw data points

explanation: Relative frequency tells you what fraction or percentage of your total group falls into a specific category. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h4)

question: When should you group continuous numbers into class intervals for a frequency table?

options.A: When the range of observed values is very wide
options.B: When the data measured is strictly nominal scale
options.C: When the total sample size is less than five
options.D: When all participants share the exact same score

explanation: Grouping numbers into intervals keeps your table short and readable when your data spans a large numerical range. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why do we leave spaces between the bars in a bar chart?

options.A: To indicate that the underlying data is continuous
options.B: To represent missing values within the data set
options.C: To show that the categories are separate and distinct
options.D: To leave room for writing numerical percentages

explanation: The gaps between bars show that each category is a separate, standalone group rather than part of a continuous flow. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which graph is best for showing a nominal variable with twelve different categories?

options.A: A stem-and-leaf plot
options.B: A frequency polygon
options.C: A pie chart
options.D: A bar chart

explanation: Bar charts remain easy to read even with many categories, whereas pie charts get too crowded after about five slices. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the main visual difference between a bar chart and a histogram?

options.A: Histograms use circles while bar charts use rectangular bars
options.B: Histograms can only display two categories at a time
options.C: Bar charts display continuous data while histograms show nominal data
options.D: Histogram bars touch each other, while bar chart bars have gaps

explanation: Histogram bars touch because they measure continuous data, while bar chart bars have gaps for separate categories. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h6)

question: What key information does a box plot give you about a set of numbers?

options.A: Exact frequency of every individual observation
options.B: Percentage breakdown of nominal categories
options.C: Cause-and-effect relationship between variables
options.D: Median, spread, and potential outliers

explanation: Box plots use quartiles to show the middle value, how spread out the data is, and any extreme values. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is an outlier in a research data set?

options.A: The exact midpoint value of a frequency distribution
options.B: A categorical variable measured on a nominal scale
options.C: A missing data point caused by a skipped interview question
options.D: An extreme value that differs significantly from other observations

explanation: Outliers are data points that sit far away from the rest of the group and can heavily skew your calculations. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why must a researcher check an outlier carefully before deleting it?

options.A: Removing data points is strictly illegal in all health research
options.B: It might represent a genuine, important clinical finding rather than an error
options.C: It guarantees that the resulting data will be normally distributed
options.D: It automatically converts ordinal data into continuous scale data

explanation: Some extreme scores reflect real, severe patient conditions rather than typing mistakes, so deleting them can throw away true evidence. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h7)

question: What is the main reason for removing names and personal details from research data?

options.A: To protect patient confidentiality and privacy
options.B: To convert qualitative text into ratio scales
options.C: To eliminate the need for frequency tables
options.D: To increase the speed of statistical software

explanation: De-identification strips away personal details so patient health information stays private and secure. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h8)

question: How should a researcher store the master list that connects patient names to study ID numbers?

options.A: Write it directly on all completed paper questionnaires
options.B: Publish it alongside the final research paper for verification
options.C: Discard it immediately before any data cleaning takes place
options.D: Store it in a separate, encrypted file away from analytical data

explanation: Keeping the master key file separate and encrypted stops unauthorized people from linking your research data back to real patients. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of data interpretation in nursing research?

options.A: Writing the initial proposal for a study
options.B: Recruiting patients for clinical trials
options.C: Assigning meaning to collected research findings
options.D: Collecting raw numbers from hospital wards

explanation: Data interpretation focuses on looking at processed data to understand what the results actually mean for patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why must raw research data undergo interpretation before clinical application?

options.A: Raw numbers alone do not automatically improve patient care
options.B: Ethical boards forbid using raw data directly in wards
options.C: Unprocessed data is always mathematically incorrect
options.D: Hospital management requires all data to be converted into charts

explanation: Data must be analyzed and translated into meaningful insights before clinicians can safely apply the findings to practice. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the first step performed on quantitative data before analysis begins?

options.A: Cleaning and structuring the data
options.B: Destroying incomplete surveys
options.C: Publishing the final results
options.D: Interpreting the p-values

explanation: Data cleaning and structuring involve checking for errors, missing values, and coding numbers properly before running statistics. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h2)

question: A researcher notices several blank responses in returned questionnaires. What should be done first?

options.A: Ignore the blanks and calculate final percentages
options.B: Identify missing values and address them according to the study protocol
options.C: Throw away the entire batch of questionnaires immediately
options.D: Guess the missing answers based on other patient files

explanation: Proper data preparation requires identifying missing values so they can be handled correctly without biasing the results. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h2)

question: What does the median represent in a set of healthcare data?

options.A: The exact middle value in an ordered dataset
options.B: The average score calculated for all patients
options.C: The most frequent symptom reported by patients
options.D: The total spread of values around the mean

explanation: The median divides a ranked dataset into two equal halves, making it reliable when extreme values are present. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which descriptive statistic is most easily distorted by extreme high or low values?

options.A: Mode
options.B: Median
options.C: Mean
options.D: Range midpoint

explanation: Because the mean includes every value in its mathematical calculation, a few extreme outliers can pull the average significantly higher or lower. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h3)

question: What does a standard p-value of less than 0.05 indicate in research?

options.A: The result is unlikely to be due to random chance
options.B: There is a 95 percent error rate in the data
options.C: The study sample size was too small to be valid
options.D: The clinical intervention caused direct patient harm

explanation: A p-value below 0.05 serves as the conventional threshold to reject the idea that findings happened purely by luck. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why must a nurse be cautious when a research paper highlights a statistically significant finding?

options.A: P-values above 0.05 are actually the safest to apply
options.B: Statistical significance does not always mean clinical importance
options.C: Significant results are always caused by measurement errors
options.D: Statistically significant data cannot be published in journals

explanation: A mathematical difference can be proven real by a study while remaining too small to change actual bedside nursing care. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the final synthesized product of qualitative data analysis called?

options.A: Means
options.B: Themes
options.C: P-values
options.D: Outliers

explanation: Qualitative analysis moves from raw text codes to categories and ultimately culminates in overarching descriptive themes. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h5)

question: How does qualitative data interpretation differ fundamentally from quantitative analysis?

options.A: It completely avoids reading transcripts or written notes
options.B: It relies entirely on complex mathematical formulas and standard deviations
options.C: It focuses on capturing human experiences and meanings rather than numbers
options.D: It proves cause-and-effect relationships through laboratory trials

explanation: Qualitative data deals with words and lived experiences, seeking to understand depth and context rather than measuring quantities. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h5)

question: A primary health clinic considers adopting a new triage protocol tested in a large tertiary hospital. What is the most important factor to check first?

options.A: If the research paper used a p-value of exactly 0.01
options.B: Whether the original study had more than one thousand subjects
options.C: Whether the clinic has similar resources and patient demographics
options.D: If the hospital researchers were registered nurses

explanation: Clinical contextualization requires checking if study settings and patient populations align with local real-world practice environments. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h6)

question: What does contextualizing research results mean for a practicing nurse?

options.A: Translating all foreign research papers into local languages
options.B: Repeating the exact research study inside a hospital ward
options.C: Evaluating how study findings fit local resource limits and patient needs
options.D: Accepting every published guideline without questioning the methods

explanation: Contextualization ensures that evidence is suitable and practical for the specific clinical environment where the nurse works. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is a confounding factor in healthcare research?

options.A: An unmeasured variable that distorts the true study relationship
options.B: A missing page in a published nursing journal
options.C: A mathematical error made during the calculation of a mean
options.D: The exact middle value found in quantitative datasets

explanation: Confounders are hidden variables that can make an intervention look effective or harmful when something else is actually responsible. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why must researchers explicitly state the limitations of their study?

options.A: To prove that no confounding factors existed in the sample
options.B: To eliminate the need for future replication studies
options.C: To show transparency about potential flaws and biases in the findings
options.D: To guarantee that the paper will be accepted by medical journals

explanation: Acknowledging limitations guides other clinicians on how cautiously they should interpret and apply the study results. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the final goal of interpreting data in nursing research?

options.A: Translating findings into clinical practice and bedside protocols
options.B: Increasing the number of published papers in journals
options.C: Writing long statistical tables for university libraries
options.D: Reducing the budget required for hospital equipment

explanation: Data interpretation is only useful when it leads to evidence-based recommendations that improve actual patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h8)

question: What makes an evidence-based recommendation strong for clinical use?

options.A: It is directly supported by analyzed data and is feasible to implement
options.B: It was written by a professor without input from bedside nurses
options.C: It costs no money to introduce into a hospital ward
options.D: It relies entirely on personal opinions rather than data

explanation: Good recommendations must stem logically from solid data analysis while remaining practical for everyday nursing workflows. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of data presentation in nursing research?

options.A: To hide incomplete data from the ethical board
options.B: To replace the need for a formal literature review
options.C: To increase the total word count of the study
options.D: To make raw findings accessible and understandable

explanation: Data presentation organizes complex findings so readers can easily grasp the clinical implications. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why must raw data be organized before clinical application?

options.A: Hospital management requires all reports to be typed
options.B: Raw numbers automatically violate patient confidentiality rules
options.C: Unorganized data makes spotting clinical trends impossible
options.D: Journals refuse to publish studies with fewer tables

explanation: Structured presentation allows nurses and researchers to identify patterns that impact patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h1)

question: When should a researcher use a textual description instead of a table?

options.A: When comparing percentages across ten different hospitals
options.B: When displaying a massive multi-variable demographic grid
options.C: When showing patient vital sign trends over five days
options.D: When presenting one or two isolated figures

explanation: Small amounts of data are best communicated directly within the narrative text without needing a separate table. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h2)

question: Graphs are superior to tables for which specific task?

options.A: Showing overall trends and patterns at a glance
options.B: Providing detailed demographic breakdown of every participant
options.C: Storing raw uncalculated survey responses securely
options.D: Listing exact numerical values for precise calculations

explanation: Visual formats like graphs allow the reader to immediately see the general direction and shape of the data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h2)

question: What design element should be avoided when creating statistical tables?

options.A: Vertical internal borders
options.B: Clearly labeled column headers
options.C: Defined units of measurement
options.D: Concise table titles

explanation: Modern formatting standards recommend omitting vertical gridlines to keep tables clean and easy to read. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why must totals and percentages be clearly distinguished in a table?

options.A: To hide missing values from external reviewers
options.B: To prevent clinical readers from misinterpreting the data
options.C: To satisfy strict page budget limits set by journals
options.D: To ensure the statistical software runs without errors

explanation: Clear distinction between raw counts and calculated percentages stops readers from confusing sample sizes with proportions. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h3)

question: What type of graph is best suited for showing changes over time?

options.A: Scatter plot
options.B: Line graph
options.C: Frequency polygon
options.D: Pie chart

explanation: Line graphs connect data points across sequential time intervals, making continuous trends easy to follow. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h4)

question: Truncating the baseline axis on a bar chart creates what problem?

options.A: It increases the total number of survey participants
options.B: It changes nominal data into ordinal data
options.C: It hides the standard deviation from the reader
options.D: It exaggerates small differences between categories

explanation: Starting an axis above zero visually distorts proportions, making minor variations look dramatic. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary basis for presenting qualitative research results?

options.A: Cross-tabulated frequency distributions
options.B: Correlation coefficients and regression lines
options.C: Thematic analysis and narrative summaries
options.D: P-values and confidence intervals

explanation: Qualitative data focuses on words, meanings, and recurring themes rather than numerical calculations. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why must qualitative researchers be cautious when selecting participant quotes?

options.A: Long quotes automatically violate institutional review board rules
options.B: Participant quotes must be translated into numerical scores first
options.C: Direct speech cannot be published in peer-reviewed journals
options.D: Quotes should represent broader consensus rather than outliers

explanation: Using only extreme or unusual quotes distorts the true meaning of the collective participant experience. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is cherry-picking in the context of research presentation?

options.A: Reporting only favorable data while ignoring contradictory findings
options.B: Choosing high-impact nursing journals for final publication
options.C: Gathering participant feedback before starting the study
options.D: Selecting the best graphic software for drawing scatter plots

explanation: Selective reporting of positive results while hiding negative outcomes violates core research ethics. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is it necessary to report findings that lack statistical significance?

options.A: Ethical boards require all studies to prove their initial hypothesis
options.B: Journals charge higher fees for statistically insignificant papers
options.C: Insignificant data can always be recalculated until it becomes valid
options.D: Withholding negative results distorts the overall evidence base

explanation: Publishing all planned outcomes prevents publication bias and gives an honest picture of clinical interventions. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of the discussion of findings section?

options.A: To explain the meaning of the results
options.B: To list every statistical test performed
options.C: To present new raw data from interviews
options.D: To outline the broad research methodology

explanation: The discussion section focuses on interpreting what the data means rather than introducing new information. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why should a researcher avoid presenting new data in the discussion chapter?

options.A: Journal word counts restrict extra paragraphs
options.B: Participants did not consent to late additions
options.C: New data belongs in the results section
options.D: Ethical boards prohibit adding extra information

explanation: Data gathering must conclude before the results and discussion phases begin to maintain analytical integrity. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h1)

question: What should be avoided when summarizing key results in the discussion?

options.A: Exhaustive numerical and statistical details
options.B: Outlines of major trends found
options.C: Mentions of secondary outcomes
options.D: A recap of primary research questions

explanation: Summaries highlight the main takeaways without repeating every single number from the results chapter. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h2)

question: A nurse researcher includes a brief recap of primary outcomes at the start of the discussion to achieve what goal?

options.A: Remind the reader of empirical outcomes
options.B: Hide errors made during data collection
options.C: Prove that the sample size was large
options.D: Replace the entire results chapter

explanation: A short summary bridges the gap between raw data presentation and subsequent deep interpretation. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h2)

question: What does aligning new research findings with past studies help to establish?

options.A: The speed of patient discharge
options.B: The exact cost of hospital equipment
options.C: The validity of the intervention
options.D: The elimination of all bias

explanation: Agreement with previous credible literature builds confidence in the reliability and validity of the new findings. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h3)

question: A nurse researcher finds that patient satisfaction scores contradict a widely accepted foreign study. What is the best initial step?

options.A: Explore potential reasons like local cultural nuances
options.B: Throw away the data because it disagrees
options.C: Change the numbers to match the foreign study
options.D: Assume the previous researchers were incompetent

explanation: Contradictory findings require careful contextual examination rather than dismissal or falsification of data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the correct approach when a researcher encounters unexpected or surprising results?

options.A: Blame the research participants for lying
options.B: Pretend the anomaly never appeared in print
options.C: Transparently analyze why the data turned out differently
options.D: Delete the unexpected data points immediately

explanation: Scientific integrity requires open discussion of anomalies rather than concealing uncomfortable data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why are unexpected outcomes valuable to the nursing profession?

options.A: They prove that standard nursing theories are useless
options.B: They eliminate the need for future data collection
options.C: They can reveal hidden variables and emerging care trends
options.D: They guarantee immediate promotion for the nurse

question: Why must a research discussion connect findings to real-world hospital policies?

question: Why does unpublished research fail to change patient care?

question: What is the primary goal of a research critique in nursing?
